concepts.title: Why measure instead of eyeballing?
concepts.body: Numbers make change visible — to you, the patient and the referrer. A measure is only useful if it is **repeatable**: same landmarks, same position, same tape tension, same tester when possible.
concepts.ur: Andaze ke bajaye naapna — taake behtari ya kharabi number mein nazar aaye. Har dafa wohi landmarks, position aur tension.

concepts.title: Tape-measure rules
bullets: Mark landmarks with a skin pen before measuring
Measure both sides at matched levels
Tape flat and snug — not indenting the skin
Take two readings and average them
concepts.body: Five habits that make tape measures reliable:

concepts.title: True vs apparent leg length
concepts.body: **True** (ASIS → medial malleolus) measures the bones. **Apparent** (umbilicus → medial malleolus) adds the effect of pelvic tilt. Equal true + unequal apparent = **functional** difference. Unequal true = **structural** — then find which bone with the Galeazzi test.

concepts.title: Measuring swelling
concepts.body: Choose the tool that fits the region: **figure-of-eight** for the ankle, **joint-line girth plus the sweep test** for the knee, **serial circumferences or volume** for lymphoedema, and **calf girth 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity** when screening for DVT.

concepts.title: What difference matters?

head: Measure
Meaningful difference
rows: > 2 cm at a point or > 10% volume

concepts.body: Use these thresholds — smaller changes may be measurement error.

concepts.title: Reliability: same tester, same method
concepts.body: Inter-tester error is larger than intra-tester error. Re-measure with the **same protocol** (and ideally the same person), and document the landmarks so a colleague can repeat it exactly.

concepts.title: Measurements that change management today
bullets: Calf > 3 cm larger with tenderness after surgery → suspected DVT: urgent referral
Rapid knee swelling within 2 hours of injury → haemarthrosis: imaging
Reduced chest expansion + occiput-to-wall gap + inflammatory back pain → rheumatology
Rapidly increasing arm girth after breast cancer treatment → lymphoedema service

concepts.title: From number to plan
concepts.body: A measurement only matters if it changes what you do: a 2.5 cm structural leg-length difference with back pain → trial heel raise; quadriceps wasting → progressive strengthening and re-measure in 4 weeks; low grip strength in an older adult → sarcopenia screen and resistance training.

cards.front: What does the True leg length assess?
cards.back: Structural (bony) leg-length difference

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the True leg length?
cards.back: ASIS to the medial malleolus

cards.front: How do you perform the True leg length?
cards.back: Supine, pelvis level, legs parallel in the same position; tape from the ASIS to the tip of the medial malleolus, both sides, twice

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the True leg length?
cards.back: A difference over about 1–1.5 cm is usually meaningful (over 2 cm often needs a heel raise)

cards.front: Common error in the True leg length?
cards.back: Pelvis tilted or the legs abducted differently; tape crossing the hip at an angle

cards.front: What does the Apparent leg length assess?
cards.back: Functional leg-length difference from pelvic obliquity

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Apparent leg length?
cards.back: Umbilicus (or xiphisternum) to the medial malleolus

cards.front: How do you perform the Apparent leg length?
cards.back: Supine with the legs parallel and in line with the trunk; tape from the umbilicus to each medial malleolus

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Apparent leg length?
cards.back: Unequal apparent but equal true lengths = functional difference (pelvic obliquity, adductor contracture, scoliosis)

cards.front: Common error in the Apparent leg length?
cards.back: Comparing it with a true length taken in a different leg position

cards.front: What does the Galeazzi (Allis) test assess?
cards.back: Whether shortening is in the femur or the tibia

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Galeazzi (Allis) test?
cards.back: Heights and positions of the two knees in hook-lying

cards.front: How do you perform the Galeazzi (Allis) test?
cards.back: Supine, hips 45° and knees 90° flexed, feet together flat on the plinth; compare knee heights from the front and the side

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Galeazzi (Allis) test?
cards.back: One knee lower = shorter tibia; one knee further back (side view) = shorter femur or hip dislocation

cards.front: Common error in the Galeazzi (Allis) test?
cards.back: Feet not level or together; pelvis rotated

cards.front: What does the Standing block method assess?
cards.back: Leg-length difference in standing

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Standing block method?
cards.back: Iliac crest (or PSIS) heights in standing

cards.front: How do you perform the Standing block method?
cards.back: Place graded blocks under the shorter leg until the iliac crests are level; the block height equals the difference

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Standing block method?
cards.back: The block height that levels the crests gives the functional difference to correct

cards.front: Common error in the Standing block method?
cards.back: Knees bent or uneven foot pronation not controlled

cards.front: What does the Thigh circumference assess?
cards.back: Quadriceps wasting (or thigh swelling)

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Thigh circumference?
cards.back: Fixed distances (e.g. 5, 10 and 15 cm) above the superior pole of the patella

cards.front: How do you perform the Thigh circumference?
cards.back: Supine, knee straight and relaxed; mark matching levels on both legs; tape snug, not indenting, perpendicular to the thigh

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Thigh circumference?
cards.back: A side difference over about 1–2 cm suggests wasting (or swelling) — track it over time

cards.front: Common error in the Thigh circumference?
cards.back: Measuring at different levels each session, contracting the quadriceps, pulling the tape tight

cards.front: What does the Knee circumference (effusion) assess?
cards.back: Knee joint swelling (effusion)

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Knee circumference (effusion)?
cards.back: Joint line at mid-patella level

cards.front: How do you perform the Knee circumference (effusion)?
cards.back: Supine, knee straight; tape around the joint line at mid-patella on both knees, then perform the sweep (stroke) test

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Knee circumference (effusion)?
cards.back: Larger girth with a positive sweep or patellar tap test = intra-articular effusion

cards.front: Common error in the Knee circumference (effusion)?
cards.back: Confusing joint effusion with soft-tissue (pre-patellar) swelling

cards.front: What does the Calf circumference assess?
cards.back: Calf swelling (e.g. DVT) or calf wasting

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Calf circumference?
cards.back: 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity

cards.front: How do you perform the Calf circumference?
cards.back: Supine, leg relaxed; measure both calves at 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Calf circumference?
cards.back: Calf more than 3 cm larger than the other side scores a point on the Wells DVT score

cards.front: Common error in the Calf circumference?
cards.back: Measuring each side at a different level

cards.front: What does the Figure-of-eight ankle measure assess?
cards.back: Ankle swelling after sprain or surgery

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Figure-of-eight ankle measure?
cards.back: Lateral malleolus, tibialis anterior tendon, navicular tuberosity, base of the 5th metatarsal, medial malleolus

cards.front: How do you perform the Figure-of-eight ankle measure?
cards.back: Ankle neutral; tape from the lateral malleolus across the instep, under the arch, back across the ankle front, behind the Achilles and back to the start

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Figure-of-eight ankle measure?
cards.back: Compare sides; a change of about 1 cm is beyond measurement error

cards.front: Common error in the Figure-of-eight ankle measure?
cards.back: Changing the tape path or tension between sessions

cards.front: What does the Arm circumference (lymphoedema) assess?
cards.back: Arm lymphoedema (e.g. after breast cancer surgery)

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Arm circumference (lymphoedema)?
cards.back: Points every 4 cm from the wrist up the arm, matched on both sides

cards.front: How do you perform the Arm circumference (lymphoedema)?
cards.back: Measure circumference at each point and calculate limb volume (truncated-cone formula), or use water displacement

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Arm circumference (lymphoedema)?
cards.back: More than 2 cm difference at any point, or more than 10% (about 200 mL) volume difference, suggests lymphoedema

cards.front: Common error in the Arm circumference (lymphoedema)?
cards.back: Starting from a different landmark each session; ignoring the normal dominant-arm difference

cards.front: What does the Upper-limb length assess?
cards.back: Arm or forearm shortening (fracture malunion, growth)

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Upper-limb length?
cards.back: Acromion to lateral epicondyle (arm); lateral epicondyle to radial styloid (forearm)

cards.front: How do you perform the Upper-limb length?
cards.back: Arm by the side, elbow straight; measure each segment on both sides

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Upper-limb length?
cards.back: A side difference shows which segment is short, e.g. after a malunited fracture

cards.front: Common error in the Upper-limb length?
cards.back: Elbow bent or shoulder elevated while measuring

cards.front: What does the Chest expansion assess?
cards.back: Rib-cage (thoracic) expansion

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Chest expansion?
cards.back: 4th intercostal space (nipple line) and the xiphisternum

cards.front: How do you perform the Chest expansion?
cards.back: Tape around the chest; measure at full breath out and full breath in — the difference is the expansion

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Chest expansion?
cards.back: Usually 2.5–5 cm or more; under 2.5 cm is reduced (e.g. axial spondyloarthritis)

cards.front: Common error in the Chest expansion?
cards.back: Tape slipping or the patient lifting the shoulders

cards.front: What does the Modified Schober test assess?
cards.back: Lumbar flexion range

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Modified Schober test?
cards.back: Lumbosacral junction (dimples of Venus), with marks 5 cm below and 10 cm above

cards.front: How do you perform the Modified Schober test?
cards.back: Standing, mark the three points; bend forward as far as possible with knees straight and re-measure the 15 cm distance

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Modified Schober test?
cards.back: An increase of about 5 cm or more is normal; less than 4 cm suggests reduced lumbar flexion

cards.front: Common error in the Modified Schober test?
cards.back: Marking the wrong spinal level or letting the knees bend

cards.front: What does the Occiput-to-wall distance assess?
cards.back: Fixed thoracic kyphosis or cervical flexion deformity

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Occiput-to-wall distance?
cards.back: Back of the head (occiput) and the wall

cards.front: How do you perform the Occiput-to-wall distance?
cards.back: Heels and back against the wall, chin level; try to touch the wall with the back of the head; measure any gap

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Occiput-to-wall distance?
cards.back: Normal is 0 cm; any gap suggests fixed kyphosis (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis, vertebral fractures)

cards.front: Common error in the Occiput-to-wall distance?
cards.back: Lifting the chin (extending the neck) to reach the wall

cards.front: What does the BMI and waist circumference assess?
cards.back: Body composition and cardiometabolic risk

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the BMI and waist circumference?
cards.back: Waist midway between the lowest rib and the iliac crest

cards.front: How do you perform the BMI and waist circumference?
cards.back: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height² (m²); waist measured at the end of a normal breath out

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the BMI and waist circumference?
cards.back: Asian cut-offs: BMI 23+ overweight, 27.5+ obese; waist ≥ 90 cm (men) or ≥ 80 cm (women) = raised risk in South Asians

cards.front: Common error in the BMI and waist circumference?
cards.back: Measuring the waist over clothing or at a different level each time

cards.front: What does the Grip strength (hand dynamometer) assess?
cards.back: Hand grip strength — a marker of overall strength and sarcopenia

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Grip strength (hand dynamometer)?
cards.back: Jamar dynamometer handle at position 2

cards.front: How do you perform the Grip strength (hand dynamometer)?
cards.back: Seated, shoulder by the side, elbow at 90°, forearm neutral; best (or mean) of 3 maximal squeezes each hand

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Grip strength (hand dynamometer)?
cards.back: Below 27 kg (men) or 16 kg (women) = low strength (EWGSOP2 sarcopenia criteria)

cards.front: Common error in the Grip strength (hand dynamometer)?
cards.back: Changing elbow or wrist position between trials; no rest between squeezes

cards.front: What does the Navicular drop assess?
cards.back: Medial arch collapse (pronation) under load

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Navicular drop?
cards.back: Navicular tuberosity

cards.front: How do you perform the Navicular drop?
cards.back: Sitting with the subtalar joint neutral, mark navicular height; stand relaxed and re-measure — the difference is the drop

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Navicular drop?
cards.back: More than about 10 mm = excessive pronation

cards.front: Common error in the Navicular drop?
cards.back: Not finding subtalar neutral, or weight uneven between the feet

cards.front: What does the Q-angle assess?
cards.back: Quadriceps line of pull on the patella

cards.front: Landmarks or set-up for the Q-angle?
cards.back: ASIS, centre of the patella and tibial tuberosity

cards.front: How do you perform the Q-angle?
cards.back: Supine (or standing), knee straight, quadriceps relaxed; goniometer axis on the patella centre, arms to the ASIS and the tibial tuberosity

cards.front: What result is normal or significant for the Q-angle?
cards.back: About 13° in men and 18° in women; larger angles are linked with patellar maltracking

cards.front: Common error in the Q-angle?
cards.back: Quadriceps contracted or the foot rotated

cards.front: True leg length is measured from…
cards.back: ASIS to medial malleolus. ASIS → medial malleolus = bony length.

cards.front: Which measurement screens for a DVT?
cards.back: Calf circumference 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. > 3 cm larger scores on the Wells DVT score.

cards.front: Which measurement best tracks ankle swelling?
cards.back: Figure-of-eight method. Reliable and quick for ankle oedema.

cards.front: Why measure both sides?
cards.back: The other side is the patient's own normal. Side-to-side comparison controls for body size.

cards.front: Grip strength is measured with a…
cards.back: Hand dynamometer. E.g. a Jamar dynamometer.

cards.front: Unequal apparent leg length with equal true leg length means…
cards.back: A functional difference (pelvic obliquity). The bones are equal; the pelvis is tilted.

cards.front: For thigh girth you should…
cards.back: Mark fixed distances above the patella on both legs. Fixed, matched landmarks make it repeatable.

cards.front: Chest expansion is calculated as…
cards.back: Full inspiration minus full expiration girth. Difference between maximal in and out.

cards.front: In the Galeazzi test, one knee is lower when viewed from the front. This suggests…
cards.back: A shorter tibia. Lower knee = tibia; knee further back = femur.

cards.front: A Modified Schober increase of 2.5 cm is…
cards.back: Reduced lumbar flexion. Normal is about 5 cm or more.

cards.front: Grip strength of 22 kg in a 70-year-old man is…
cards.back: Low — below the 27 kg sarcopenia threshold. EWGSOP2: < 27 kg men, < 16 kg women.

cards.front: A South Asian woman has a waist of 86 cm. This is…
cards.back: Above the 80 cm risk threshold. IDF South Asian cut-off: ≥ 80 cm (women).

cards.front: Lymphoedema is suggested by a volume difference over about…
cards.back: 10% (≈ 200 mL). > 10% volume or > 2 cm at any point.

cards.front: Day 6 after knee replacement: right calf 4 cm larger than left, warm and tender, pitting oedema. — What do you do?
cards.back: Stop treatment and refer urgently for DVT assessment. Calf > 3 cm + tenderness + oedema after surgery = suspected DVT.

cards.front: Back pain; true leg length R 88 cm, L 85.5 cm; apparent lengths differ similarly. — Best action?
cards.back: Structural 2.5 cm difference — consider a heel raise and locate it (Galeazzi). Unequal true lengths = structural; 2.5 cm often warrants a raise.

cards.front: Footballer: knee swelled within 1 hour of a twisting injury; joint-line girth +3 cm, positive patellar tap. — What does it suggest?
cards.back: Haemarthrosis — likely ACL tear, fracture or patellar dislocation: refer for imaging. Rapid effusion = blood in the joint.

cards.front: 6 weeks after ACL reconstruction: thigh girth 3 cm smaller 10 cm above the patella. — Interpretation and plan?
cards.back: Quadriceps wasting — progress strengthening and confirm with strength testing. Girth loss = wasting; strength testing confirms.

cards.front: A 25-year-old man: inflammatory back pain, chest expansion 1.5 cm, occiput-to-wall 4 cm. — Next step?
cards.back: Refer to rheumatology for possible axial spondyloarthritis. Reduced expansion + fixed kyphosis + inflammatory pain.

cards.front: Post-mastectomy, the affected arm is 2.8 cm larger at 10 cm above the wrist; feels heavy. — Most likely and action?
cards.back: Early lymphoedema — refer to the lymphoedema service for compression and exercise. > 2 cm difference with heaviness = lymphoedema.

cards.front: Why record exact landmarks and positions in your notes?
cards.back: So the measurement can be repeated reliably by you or a colleague. Reproducibility makes change meaningful.

cards.front: An 80-year-old: grip 14 kg, gait speed 0.7 m/s, recent weight loss. — What does this suggest?
cards.back: Probable sarcopenia/frailty — resistance training, nutrition review and medical review. Low grip + slow gait = sarcopenia/frailty markers.

cards.front: Apparent leg length: left shorter by 3 cm; true lengths equal; left hip held in 15° adduction. — Cause?
cards.back: Left hip adduction contracture tilting the pelvis. An adducted hip makes that leg appear shorter.

cards.front: Ankle sprain: figure-of-eight 54.5 cm today, 55.0 cm last week. — Interpretation?
cards.back: Change is within measurement error — not yet a meaningful reduction. A change under about 1 cm may be error.

cards.front: True leg length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Then locate it: compare knee heights in hook-lying (Galeazzi) to see whether the femur or the tibia is short.

cards.front: Apparent leg length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: A hip held in adduction (e.g. contracture) makes that leg look shorter even when the bones are equal.

cards.front: Galeazzi (Allis) test — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Also used to screen infants for developmental dysplasia of the hip — but bilateral dislocation gives a false negative.

cards.front: Standing block method — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Often more accurate than tape measures; an X-ray scanogram is the gold standard.

cards.front: Thigh circumference — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Wasting starts within days of knee injury or surgery. Girth is only a proxy — confirm with strength testing.

cards.front: Knee circumference (effusion) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Rapid swelling within about 2 hours of injury suggests haemarthrosis — ACL tear, fracture or patellar dislocation.

cards.front: Calf circumference — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Calf swelling, tenderness along the deep veins and pitting oedema after surgery = suspected DVT: stop, don't massage, refer urgently.

cards.front: Figure-of-eight ankle measure — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Highly reliable and much quicker than water-displacement volumetry.

cards.front: Arm circumference (lymphoedema) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Measure before surgery for a baseline. Early detection allows compression and exercise before fibrosis develops.

cards.front: Upper-limb length — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Whole-limb length runs from the acromion to the tip of the middle finger.

cards.front: Chest expansion — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Reduced chest expansion in a young adult with inflammatory back pain is a classic spondyloarthritis sign.

cards.front: Modified Schober test — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: The 'modified-modified' version marks the PSIS line and 15 cm above — choose one version and keep to it.

cards.front: Occiput-to-wall distance — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: The tragus-to-wall distance (part of BASMI) follows the same idea.

cards.front: BMI and waist circumference — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: BMI misclassifies muscular people and older adults; waist circumference adds central-fat risk.

cards.front: Grip strength (hand dynamometer) — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Low grip strength predicts disability and mortality. The dominant hand is usually about 10% stronger.

cards.front: Navicular drop — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: Pair it with the Foot Posture Index in medial tibial stress syndrome or patellofemoral pain.

cards.front: Q-angle — clinical note: what must you remember?
cards.back: A static Q-angle predicts little on its own — dynamic knee valgus during movement matters more.
